EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL (NO 2)
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I move, That the Education
Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read a first time.  I nominate the Education and Science
Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time I intend to move that the bill be
reported by 21 July 2014.
Our Government has  a comprehensive, successful, and sustainable education plan.
We want every New Zealand child to get a better education so that they can be
successful here, at home in New Zealand, as well as globally competitive. This
Government is investing in an educati on system that gives students and young people
the skills that they need to achieve success in education and in life. This is why we are
introducing legislation that sets up the education profession with an independent entity
as the cornerstone of our qual ity teaching agenda, to ensure our education system meets
the challenges and opportunities of the modern learning context. This will promote
educational leadership, accountability, and high standards within the education system;
help to drive continuous im provement by strengthening and streamlining quality
assurance processes; and establish a regulatory framework for the protection of children
and for discipline —for the highest and safest behaviour. My colleague the Hon Steven
Joyce will speak in more detai l about the tertiary and international education aspects of
the bill.
The Government is focused on strengthening and valuing the education profession.
Earlier this year our Prime Minister announced an investment of $359 million for
teaching and leadership  career pathways that will create four new teaching and
leadership roles in schools. These roles will recognise and use talent where it is needed
most. They will be implemented from next year to support communities of schools
across the country. Importantl y, the pathways will have a focus on supporting teachers
to collaborate to lift achievement.
This year we are reviewing professional learning and development for the
compulsory school sector. This month we are hosting the International Summit on the
Teaching Profession here in Wellington. We expect to host Ministers of education from
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16685
the top-performing education systems from all a round the world . At the same time we
are hosting education festivals in Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch  to showcase
school best practice to each other, to parents, and to the community and to celebrate
what is happening in our schools. We have instituted the inaugural Prime Minister’s
Education Excellence Awards, to be awarded in June this year.
We want to build on the good  practice that occurs in schools every day and support
the system to promote high professional standards and accountability. The Education
Council of Aotearoa New Zealand  is integral to our plan to value and strengthen the
teaching profession. The bill est ablishes the Education Council of Aotearoa New
Zealand, EDUCANZ, which will be a new professional body for the education
profession, replacing the existing New Zealand Teachers Council. I would like, at this
time, to record my thanks to the New Zealand Tea chers Council for the sterling work
that it has done over the duration of its existence and to thank it for the work that it will
continue to do until the new body is in place.
This bill today is the result of a 3 -year conversation. Widespread consultatio n began
in 2010 when the Education Workforce Advisory Committee wrote its report, and it
ended with the 2013 ministerial advisory group report, which led engagement on the
proposals right across the profession. EDUCANZ will lead and promote quality
teaching in New Zealand. As an independent statutory body it will focus on investing in
high-quality leadership and teaching practice across early childhood and schooling. It
will be the guardian for standards for teachers and help ensure that the aspirations we
have for educational success are realised in the day -to-day operation of our education
system. EDUCANZ will be owned by the profession and will have its needs at its heart
in the interests of quality learning and the best education for each and every child  and
young New Zealander.
The bill sets out the purposes and functions of EDUCANZ and the appointment
process for members. Members will be appointed by the Minister and will have the
skills, attributes, and credentials to lead the profession. Of the nine appointed members,
up to five will be registered teachers. Many of the functions of the new professional
body reflect that of the New Zealand Teachers Council, but it will have additional
responsibilities in providing direction for the profession. The most  important role of
EDUCANZ will be as steward and guardian of the standards of the profession.
The bill requires EDUCANZ to develop a code of conduct that must be adhered to by
every teacher in New Zealand, ensuring that there is clarity for all about the  expected
behaviour and conduct of teachers and the priority of safety for the young people in
their care. The bill promotes the safety of students through a robust regulatory
framework for teachers. Teacher registration will be separated from the issue of
practising certificates, to promote the professional value and status of those practising
certificates.
The safety of learners in our schools is an absolute priority. This Government
supports an education system that takes a robust approach to safeguardi ng children and
young people. Therefore the bill will make changes to strengthen and clarify the
disciplinary framework for teachers. To help raise public confidence in the profession,
any teacher convicted of a serious criminal offence will have their reg istration
cancelled. EDUCANZ will have an explicit function to monitor and enforce the
mandatory reporting requirements relating to teacher misconduct. Likewise,
streamlining the powers of the complaints assessment committee will ensure that
appropriate disciplinary measures are taken in a timely manner. The Education Council
Disciplinary Tribunal can suspend a teacher’s practising certificate if the safety of
children or the reputation of the teaching profession are in question. We are removing
the current 3-month maximum interim suspension.
16686 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
The bill helps us to achieve our aim of five out of five students achieving success in
education. We are committed to ensuring that our education system is well equipped to
meet the challenges of the modern learning co ntext. The Education Amendment Bill
(No 2)  helps us achieve this. We have invested significantly in consulting with
education professionals to ensure that this bill reflects both their aspirations and their
ambitions but also balances the need to ensure th at the safety of children and the
protection of parents’ interests, in terms of their children, are also safeguarded. I now
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I cal l the honourable
member Christopher Hipkins.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That is what my mother calls me when I
am being badly behaved. First of all, I suppose I should sympathise with the Minist er of
Education’s croaky voice. I am not sure whether I will get through 10 minutes today,
either. There seems to be something in the water at Parliament today.
I do want to pick up on some of the comments that the Minister made in her speech
on this bill, the Education Amendment Bill (No 2). It seems that whenever the Minister
speaks in the House about education, there needs to be some translation. When she talks
about an independent voice for teachers and a teachers’ body that is governed and
owned by the teaching profession, it is very difficult to reconcile that with the idea that
the Minister will hand -pick all the members of it. How is the profession supposed to
feel in ownership of the body if it does not actually have any say in who is governing
that body? The membership of the council is going to be exclusively determined by the
Minister. That is completely at odds with the idea that this will be a body that is owned
by the teaching profession.
The Labour Party does support an independent teaching body; whether it is called the
Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand (EDUCANZ) or something else, it does
not really matter. The principle of an independent body is something that we are
strongly in support of. However, having that body exclusively appointed by the Minister
simply is not going to lead to that. This body, to do the job that it is being tasked with,
must have the confidence and the support of the profession, because without that it
simply is not going to be able to do the job, and it is n ot going to get that support if the
teaching profession feels that the new EDUCANZ body is something that is being done
to it, rather than being done with it.
When Hekia Parata talked about this being the result of a 3 -year conversation, most
people in th e education sector would say that there is a big difference between being
talked at and spoken with. The problem is that the current Government’s approach is
very much to talk at people who are working in education, rather than have a genuine
conversation with them. I think that there should be an independent, robust education
council or teaching council that does have quite an expansive role in raising the quality
of education in New Zealand and in raising the status of the teaching profession in New
Zealand. Sadly, that is not what the Education Amendment Bill (No 2) is delivering.
When Hekia Parata mentioned briefly the changes in this bill to make tertiary
governance more effective, what she effectively meant is the removal of staff and
student represen tation. That is not going to lead to more collaboration and a more
collegial approach to educational provision. Hekia Parata talked in her speech about the
Government’s plan to introduce expert teachers. One simple question: which teachers
will not be the experts?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: The ones that aren’t raising achievement.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, the ones who are not raising achievement. Well, if they are
not raising achievement, then one has to question why they are still teac hing, and ask
whether, in fact, the Government should be focused on providing support to all teachers,
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16687
because all teachers should be expert teachers. The idea that we are going to have a two-
tier teaching profession —where if you are one of the lucky few w ho gets an expert
teacher, you get a better-quality education than all the others, who supposedly have non
- expert teachers—clearly shows that the Government has got all its priorities wrong.
When the Government talks about expert principals, what it is basically saying is:
“We will take a principal who is doing a good job of running their school, and we will
reward them for that by taking them out of their school for a couple of days a week, and
we will pretend that by being out of their school for a cou ple of days a week they can
still continue to do the good job they were doing when they were there full time.” Most
principals will say that, actually, being a good principal is more than a full -time job.
Running one school is more than a full -time job, so how on earth Hekia Parata and the
Government can think that a good principal will somehow be able to run a whole lot of
schools whilst still running their school at the same time is beyond anybody.
It is no wonder that the teaching profession and the principals are walking away from
this. They are clearly walking away from this, and we have seen that in the last few
days. They were willing to give the Government the benefit of the doubt, and in record
quick time Hekia Parata has already managed to burn th em off. She has already
managed to burn them off. The whole profession was willing to say: “Actually, let’s
work with the Government and see whether we can make this work.”, and already it is
walking away, saying: “No, this isn’t going to work.” EDUCANZ an d the future of the
teaching profession should be driven by the profession. In what other profession does
the Government dictate: “This is how you will run yourselves. This is what all of the
criteria will be.”? There are not very many. I actually think—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: The Minister already makes all the appointments, Mr Hipkins.
Read the law that your Government put in place.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I have read the Cabinet paper, I say to Hekia Parata. I have read
the Cabinet paper, thin as it was, and it was very clear that there was a very insubstantial
evidence base there. Going on holiday somewhere does not create an evidence base for
something. It seems to be that Hekia Parata thinks that just by going somewhere and
speaking to a few people, it creates an evidence base. Actually, there is a lot more to an
evidence base than that. There was a very flimsy evidence base for the proposals that
have been put forward by John Key and the National Government, and it is no wonder
that that is already starting to come unstuck.
We do need to focus on raising the quality of education in New Zealand, and that
starts by recognising the critical role of the teaching profession in setting and
maintaining the standards for the profession. Tha t is something that this Government is
not willing to do. This Government thinks that it can impose those standards on the
teaching profession, including by setting up an establishment body for the new
education council of New Zealand, which has a National Party office holder on it. If you
want to know why it is that the teaching profession baulks at the idea that the Minister
would appoint —hand-pick—the entire board of the new education council of New
Zealand, that is a pretty good example. That is a prett y good example. I actually think
that the teaching profession should have the ultimate say, or at least a significant say, on
how this body is made up. That is not something that Hekia Parata is willing to do,
because this Government thinks that it should be dictating to the teaching profession
what should be going on within the profession.
This bill, of course, entrenches —entrenches—the double standard of this
Government, where on the one hand it is talking about raising the standards for the
teaching profession and then, on the other hand, it is exempting charter schools from
those provisions. It is exempting its small group of charter schools from those
provisions. If it is really committed to raising the standard of the teaching profession,
16688 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
why would it  exempt the newest schools —the schools that it wants to expand? Why
would it say that this new model of education should be exempt from the agenda to
raise the standards in the profession? It has no good reason for doing that. This bill
simply entrenches the double standard that says that schools in the public system should
be dumped all over, as they have repeatedly been by this current Government, while the
charter schools, which the Government is hand -picking and establishing , should get a
different set of standards.
Of course, it is all spin—all this good news that we are getting from the Government
is spin. Let us not forget that this is the Government that thought that the answer to
quality teaching was increasing class sizes. This is a Government that, after a year and a
half and $43 million of taxpayers’ money being shovelled at it, still cannot get the
payroll system right—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: That you signed up, “Chippy”!

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —so that teachers actually get  paid for their work. Steven Joyce
is an absolute failure. “Mr Fix-it” still has not fixed it. A year and a half and $43 million
later, Steven Joyce’s answer is to shovel another $10 million at it and hope for the best.
Novopay does not work, and Steven Jo yce still has not fixed it. He has been an absolute
failure. “Mr Fix-it” did not fix Novopay.
Bigger class sizes, Novopay, school closures in Christchurch, national standards that
are neither national nor standard —the litany of educational failures of thi s Government
is not going to be undone by a little bit of spin work now, where the Government claims
it actually values the teaching profession. It values them so much, it is not willing to
entrust them with any decision making over the future of the teach ing profession. This
is a Government that is not willing to practise what it preaches.
This is a Government that wants to control everything. Hekia Parata wants to control
the new education council, and yet we know that the courts do not have any faith in  her
decision making, because twice she has been challenged in the courts, and twice she has
lost. She has been twice challenged in the courts, and she lost on both occasions. The
courts even went so far as to say that she had abrogated her responsibilities as a decision
maker.
Now Hekia Parata wants to have decision -making responsibilities for the whole
teaching profession. She wants to hand -pick the entire body of the new education
council. I think that is wrong. I think teachers should have a say in who  is going to be
on this new education council. The Government has no good reason for explaining why
it does not believe that. Not once has the Government put forward a compelling
argument for why this body should be exclusively appointed by the Minister of
Education.
We should be focused on raising the status of the teaching profession in New
Zealand. That means meaningful recognition for the teaching profession. It means
meaningful ongoing dialogue and discussion with people working in the teaching
profession. It means a two -way conversation, not a Minister who is preaching to them,
telling them what is best for them, and never listening.
Hon STEVEN JOYCE ( Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): I would like to thank the author of the Novopay contract, Chris Hipkins,
for that contribution. I would like to thank him for that. Unfortunately, I cannot thank
him for much else. Unfortunately, also, I do not understand his contribution. I have tried
to summarise it. I have tried to summarise it for him. It appears that he thinks that
independent teacher councils are important, but they should not be too independent.
That is the first thing he said.  He also seems to be relitigating Labour’s support for
teaching excellence. He seems to be quickly moving away from its support for teaching
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16689
excellence. But, to be fair to him, that is Labour’s “yeah, nah” approach, as exhibited in
education.
The Education Amendment Bill (No 2) is an important bill. This bill will improve
our education system. I agree with the remarks made by my colleague the Hon Hekia
Parata and I suspect I will not agree with remarks about to be made by “Jurassic” Grant
Robertson. In my speech, I would like to focus on the two areas of the bill—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What’s that, Humpty-Dumpty?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —within my portfolio of tertiary education, skills, and
employment. It is all right; I will come to you, Grant. First, let me deal with the
Government’s reforms to university and wānanga governance. These moderate but
important changes modernise councils so that they are smaller, skills -based, and can
better respond and more quickly respond to the challenges of modern -day tertiary
education. The changes will mean that the councils can more easily meet the needs of a
rapidly changing employment market; adapt to the new challenges from changing
technology, teaching, and learning; and operate more effectively in an increasingly
competitive international university environment.
There are four major changes from the current model. Firstly, councils will decrease
in size from 12 to 20 members currently to eight  to 12 members. Universities and
wānanga will choose their council size within those parameters. Secondly, council
membership requirements will be more flexible by the removal of specific
representative requirements. The current law is highly prescriptive and outdated in that
regard. Thirdly, the Minister and councils will be required to appoint members with
skills, knowledge, or experience relevant to each council’s particular needs. Fourthly,
the duties and accountabilities of individual council members w ill be clarified. That is
it. “Jurassic” Grant Robertson has been roaming the campuses, desperately trying to
wind the students up to revolt in the streets and they have largely ignored him. In fact, if
it had not been for my signing them up for the Young Nats at Victoria University’s
campus the other day, nobody would have been talking to him.
These changes will allow both universities and wānanga to recruit the expertise
needed to effectively respond to the challenges of a changing environment. Individua l
council members will get a clear picture of what is expected of them. Those who are
performing poorly will be prevented from undermining the overall performance of a
council. The changes will help address the difficulties that larger councils can have,
with timely decision-making and communication. They will bring university and
wānanga councils more in line with most other organisations in the modern world,
which have been moving towards smaller governing bodies for quite some time—many,
many years, in fact. The go vernance changes made to our polytechnic sector in 2010
have greatly contributed to the turn -round in educational and financial performance in
that sector. All university and wānanga councils will be required to have at least one
Māori member to assist the  Government’s role of raising achievement for Māori. This
will not be a significant change, as all but one do today.
The changes are particularly important for wānanga. The current governance settings
were not written with them in mind. They were asked to  adopt the university settings.
The changes will allow increased flexibility for wānanga to reflect their unique
stakeholders, particularly iwi, on their councils. I want to stress that, despite the
scaremongering of “Jurassic” Grant—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just remind the
member that the member must use an honourable member’s full name, not a nickname
or anything else. All members in this House are honourable.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I apologise, Mr Assistant Speaker. I will not refer to him in
that manner again, even though his response to these things is reasonably outdated. The
16690 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
changes will not compromise institutional autonomy or academic freedom. These
freedoms are guaranteed by section 161 of the Education Act, which is not changing, so
I can therefore save the Opposition members their breath for the rest of this debate and
the subsequent stages of this bill, because those matters are not changing. I know that
members opposite are concerned about student representation, and that is important.
Under the changes proposed in this bill councils will be free to choose to retain their
student and staff representation. I have already stated that I expect most institution s will
do just that. The key point is that they get the flexibility to determine the best make -up
of their councils; we treat them like adult organisations.
The changes proposed in the bill are the latest in a series of incremental reforms
made by the Gov ernment to improve the performance and quality of tertiary education.
We have reduced spending in low -value areas, such as student loans for people who
consistently fail their courses, and we have improved the way the system targets need.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Like people over 55. They’re terribly low value, aren’t they,
Steven—people over 55.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: We have set performance incentives on providers and
students—here comes the guy who wants to spend the money —and imp roved
information for students about the performance of providers and the employment
outcomes of their study. Interestingly, Government investment in tertiary education has
risen substantially. In 2012 we invested $2.2 billion in publicly owned tertiary
institutions. That in itself is an increase of 13.4 percent since 2008. The investment
increase in universities is higher—up 16 percent since 2008. The approach is paying off.
We achieved a record number of qualifications in 2012 —162,000. The number of
domestic students who completed a Bachelor’s degree in 2012 was the highest ever, at
25,400, up 4,790 in just 2 years —an increase of 23 percent. Right through the 2000s,
despite the buckets and buckets of money that Labour poured into this system, the
number of degree graduates flat -lined, despite these big increases in funding. So these
results are great to see, when somebody manages the tertiary education system properly
and does not rely on old fossil politicians from the student unions. Many more young
people are now moving from school to degree-level study: from 13,600 students in 2007
to 16,500 in 2012. These in clude more young Māori and Pasifika. The total number of
Māori students enrolled in total in qualifications at Bachelor’s level or higher increased
from 17,500 to 21,900 in 2012. The number of Pasifika students increased too from
I will now talk about how the bill will improve the education system’s
responsiveness to the needs of international students. International education is very
important to New Zealand. It contributes $2.6 billion a year to our economy and 28,000
jobs for New Zealanders. I thought most parties in this House supported international
education; after last week though I am not quite so sure, because the Shane Jones and
Raymond Huo thing about supporting international education one day and not the next
did send yet another confusing signal from the Opposition. The Business Growth
Agenda has set a goal of doubling the total value of New Zealand’s international
education sector to $5 billion by 2025. It is also part of our drive to be better connected
across the world. Our success as a country depends on our level of connectedness. At
the end of the day, we are a small trading nation and we need very strong links with the
world, and international education is an important way to develop those links. It
provides New Zealand with lifelong ambassadors as graduates go back to their home
countries and share their experiences with friends, family, and colleagues. It helps
enhance teaching and research, the sharing of knowledge, and the building of human
capital. We m ust take steps to ensure always that our international students have the
best possible experience while they are here. This bill adds on the reforms we have
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16691
already made and creates a new legal framework for the Code of Practice for the
Pastoral Care of In ternational Students. This will enable targeted interventions in
situations where providers are not complying with their obligations under the code. A
more effective and efficient sanction process will be introduced to ensure that code
signatories represent New Zealand education in the best possible way. It also establishes
a dedicated disputes resolution scheme, which provides international students with an
accessible and efficient forum for settling financial or contractual disputes with
providers.
The b ill also makes improvements to student fee protection, which covers both
domestic and international students. That will help reduce the compliance costs
associated with that for private training establishments. The bill strengthens the ability
of the New Z ealand Qualifications Authority to undertake quality assurance of tertiary
education organisations and streamlines the process for deregistration of private training
establishments. To protect the quality of tertiary education the bill strengthens
enforcement and offence provisions, and provides disincentives for those who seek to
avoid the consequences of poor performance. This bill is from a Government that is
doing a very good job in the education sector and a very good job in tertiary education. I
know it is galling for the Opposition, but we are receiving great results in the tertiary
sector. This bill makes important changes to the governance of our universities and
wānanga so they can respond more effectively and strategically in the modern world,
Mr Robertson—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —and it will create a more robust regulatory framework for
our international education sector. This bill is a good bill for our tertiary education
sector. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to
follow on from “Mr Fix -it”, Steven Joyce, who told us he would solve the Novopay
problems in 3 months. That is what he told us —that he would solve the Novopay
problems in 3 months. It was no t so much a case of “Can we fix it? Yes, we can.”; it
was a case of “Can we fix it? No, we can’t.”, because the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment, Steven Joyce, is responsible for the Novopay
debacle. We learnt today that Novopay has c ost another $43 million to New Zealanders
and it is why teachers continue not to be paid. What kind of Government can claim
success in education but is not paying the teachers, is not paying the staff in our schools,
and is seeing support staff in our scho ols resign because of the stress of it? Good old
“Mr Fix-it” is behind that, making sure that Novopay continues to fail.
On this side of the House we will be opposing this legislation, the Education
Amendment Bill. We will be opposing it strongly. The reforms to university governance
that are being proposed by Steven Joyce and Hekia Parata, to quote New Zealand’s
largest university, “strike at the very essence of autonomous but accountable
universities in this country.” That is a quote from the University of Auckland’s
submission on these proposals. These proposals undermine everything that universities
and tertiary education are about: being the critic and conscience of society. Steven Joyce
does not want to hear from critics. Steven Joyce wants to silence  the voices of critics of
his policies, and that is what lies behind these changes.
There is no evidence that lies behind these changes. There is no great call for the
terrible governance of universities that has driven them into the ground financially. I t
has not happened. New Zealand universities are generally performing very well. They
are adapting very well to the so -called modern world that Steven Joyce talks about.
There is no problem here. This policy is a solution in search of a problem. It is Stev en
Joyce’s ideological response to people who disagree with him. It typifies a National
16692 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
Government that does not want to hear about criticism. Be it protest at sea or protest at a
university, this Government does not want to hear from critics. It works to silence
critics by shutting them out, and we on this side of the House utterly oppose that.
There has been no evidence provided for this. We looked, and what we saw in the
regulatory impact statement were a whole lot of “could be’s”, “maybe’s” and “might
be’s”. “Current governance arrangements” —this is what the regulatory impact
statement says —“may not be optimised.” They may not support efficient decision -
making. They could result in people not making good decisions. There is no evidence; it
is made up. Steven Joyce is simply putting forward his ideological solution to a problem
that he has invented. Maybe, as he said today, large bodies in universities have
difficulty making good decisions. Maybe around the world there will be examples
where large councils are causing universities to have terrible performance.
Let us look at a few of them. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology —one of the
leading innovative research universities in the world —how many people are on its
council? Seventy-two people are on  its council. Before Steven Joyce gets too excited, I
am not proposing an increase to 72. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology seems
to be doing all right, but perhaps that is an outlier. I know, why do we not look to the
great universities, to Oxford  and Cambridge? That will give us a guide. They will have
small councils, because there is no way the Oxford and Cambridge universities could
not be making good decisions. Well, Oxford has 25 on its council.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: That’s a lot less than 72.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is. Cambridge has 23 on its council —not eight, not 12,
but 25 or 23 —and Stanford has 33. If you look at the 50 top universities in the world,
most of them still have this kind of representative mode l. Many of them have far more
than the number of councillors that are proposed in the current law in New Zealand.
There is no relationship here between universities, the size of their governing bodies,
and their success. It is just not there. There is no evidence. Steven Joyce has provided
no evidence. There is no problem with the financial performance of universities in New
Zealand, and any problems will certainly not be dealt with by more of Steven Joyce’s
mates being on the councils. There is no evidenc e that this actually supports better
learning or teaching inside an institution. There is no evidence that universities are not
responding to the modern world, that they are not looking at new ways of providing
courses, and that they are not looking at new  ways of attracting students. Steven Joyce
has made up a problem and he has no real support for this.
When they did the consultation process there were around 2,000 submissions.
Almost none of them supported any aspect of this —almost none. Of the universi ties
themselves, absolutely no one supported this whole proposal —absolutely nobody. Our
two largest universities —Auckland and Otago —have outright rejected the proposal.
They do not want it; they are happy with where they are. The excuse that the Minister
has used for the University of Canterbury looking to reduce the number on its council
down to 12, was that it could have done it under the current law. It does not even want
the law changed. Nobody wants this apart from Steven Joyce and possibly his mate Ph il
O’Reilly, who I expect will come along to the select committee and tell us what Steven
Joyce wants him to tell us. There is nobody else out there. Staff, students, and
community representatives—none of them want this.
Actually, the representative model  of governance gives universities something very
special. It gives them the ability to have at the table  the communities that they serve. If
you just want to look at it from an economic perspective, students pay a whole lot of
money to be there. Steven Joy ce might understand that argument, maybe. But beyond
that, universities have a special character. They play a special role in our society. They
are the critic and conscience of our society. They represent something that is important
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16693
about higher learning, education, and what we want for our society. The university
councils we have show that they are part of their communities. It shows that by having
the students there, by having the staff there, and by having people who come from
worker groups, employer gro ups, and the community the university is both part of and
there to serve. We think that actually makes for better decision-making.
I was on a university council myself. I know that when student voices are there it
makes a difference. I know that when staf f voices are there it makes a difference. I
actually also know that when employer and union representatives are there it makes a
difference. Better decisions are made because there is a wider representative model. It is
actually about inclusion rather than  exclusion, but this Government is all about who it
can exclude, not who it can include in the kinds of decisions that get made. Actually,
modern governance theory says that more people should be involved in decision making
in businesses. This is a tired, old policy from the 1980s. Mr Joyce might want to throw
insults around about dinosaurs and Jurassic Park . Well, he is the one bringing
something back from the 1980s, some sort of Chicago school of economics model that
says that small, by definition, must be good.
As others have said, and as I asked Mr Joyce in the House a while back, presumably
there will be some kind of policy coming from National to reduce the size of Cabinet
from 20 to eight or 12. Clearly, Cabinet as a body of 20 is not capable of maki ng good
decisions, because large bodies of 20 could not be capable of making a good decision.
Presumably, Steven Joyce will practise what he preaches in that regard—I think not.
This bill is ill -thought-out. It will cause problems. It will cause trouble. The answer
in the regulatory impact statement was to say let us manage it by saying things that will
placate people. The reality is that this will reduce the representation of key stakeholders
in a university, it will limit the range of views that are at t he table, and it will lead to
poorer governance, not better governance. The Labour Party strongly opposes this
legislation.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Tēnā
koutou e  te Whare Pāremata. The Education Amendment Bill (No 2) is a consistent
continuation of Government policy. It is a plan to further privatise the governance of
tertiary institutions, reform the Teachers Council without the support of teachers, and
continue to create two tiers and lower standards for schools such as charter schools
versus those in the State sector. Therefore, the Green Party will not be supporting this
bill. There are useful elements in small parts of the bill, but the overall thrust is
depressing. One of my colleagues will take a later call on the debacle in the tertiary
sector, the reduction of democracy, and the increasing of ministerial powers over
tertiary governance. I do agree with Grant Robertson that this is an out -of-date,
backward-looking, failed management theory, which many people have abandoned.
Inclusion, broadness, and representation are how, we all know, better decisions are
made. One of my colleagues will expand on that in her later call.
I would like to make some general com ments about the overall direction of the bill.
The overall direction is not only the National Government’s policy but also part of an
international process we are seeing that has afflicted the education sector. Education has
always been a politicised and deeply debated space, but now it is an eroded space in this
country, where concepts like education for lifelong learning and educators as the
conscience of society are being minimised and marginalised by the overarching and
depressing determination that edu cation is mainly a business. From early childhood to
the tertiary education sector, it has been carved up for profit, and the compulsory sector
is being redefined from the perspective of business efficiency and standardisation.
I would like to talk about a parent whom I met with today, who said to me that their
5-year-old had been kept in at lunchtime to improve their spelling because the school
16694 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
was worried about meeting national standards. That is a very, very depressing
experience for a parent. And a tea cher told me that she was forced to put up a picture in
her classroom of where every child was at in relation to national standards —those who
were failing, supposedly, and those who were achieving. If that is what we call expert
teaching, that is a tragedy. That teacher, who is a remarkably good teacher, is destroyed
by the introduction in her classroom of competition and the exposure of so -called
achievement for 5 -year-olds, 6 -year-olds, and 7 -year-olds. That is what I am talking
about, Minister—not that she wishes to hear it.
There is endless rhetoric in the education space about meeting student needs, creating
outcomes, and fulfilling potential for all. We can all buy in to that. But when we read
the clauses of this bill, it is pretty clear that it is ab out advancing changes that will fulfil
a very different power shift. The reform of the Teachers Council was heralded with
some excitement. Teachers expressed interest in the idea of a professional body that was
by teachers for teachers. They were intereste d in the model that would regulate and
represent them as professionals, just as medical professionals have their own
professional bodies.
However, things started to go badly awry when the transition chair of this process,
John Morris, put out a series of papers advocating right-wing education solutions, such
as performance -based pay, through The New Zealand Initiative, when he was
supposedly leading a neutral process of developing the new Education Council of
Aotearoa New Zealand. The “see no evil” Governm ent saw no conflict of interest in his
behaviour, but the teachers organisations smelt a big rat, because performance pay is
divisive, inefficient, destructive, and irrelevant to student well -being, and it should have
had no place in the discussion around the development of the new education council. It
was deeply conflicting that the transition chair actually focused on that and politicised
that process.
Now we see the enabling legislation but we do not see the robust involvement of the
broader teaching se ctor representing the concept of quality public education. The
education council is described in the bill as being “to provide leadership to teachers and
direction for the education profession:”, as well as having a number of other new roles
and responsibi lities. Who gets these roles and how they are developed is a critical
process and should not have been a politicised situation. It should have been an
inclusive and depoliticised situation. I guess the new bill could not let the new education
council be a teacher-led professional body, because then all of the provisions of the
Education Act that undermine accountability, safety, and transparency in the charter
schools would have become an even greater contradiction.
The Green Party sees no need to abandon the limited authority to teach as an
important adjunct to the essential role of the registered teacher, because that idea —the
limited authority to teach —was always based on the idea that these were people who
were studying towards an education qualificatio n but also were contributing to
classrooms. The bill sets up all kinds of structures, which we do not disagree with, to
protect children, to regulate teacher registration, and to establish a code of conduct —
note that it is not a code of ethics but a code o f conduct—but it is extraordinary that
these are not applied in other parts of the Education Act to the unregistered teaching
staff in charter schools, who will also be working with the same range of students and
who are not covered by the education counci l rules. They will have police checks, but
so should all volunteers. They might be fabulous or they might be a risk, but lowering
standards seems to be an underlying contradiction alongside double standards.
On the one hand, teachers are meant to be profe ssional leaders who get $350 million
spent on their career pathways towards executive principal, and on the other hand, in the
charter schools, in the targeting of the so -called vulnerable students, the staff do not
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16695
have to be teachers and are not covered by the codes of conduct or accountability rules
of the new education council. So it is all about tightening up the rules for teachers but
totally relaxing them for others, and that is a massive contradiction.
All students deserve an education that is libe rating, innovative, and inspiring, and of
course I agree that they are not all getting that now. I have visited the people working on
charter schools—some who are clearly motivated by the best reasons, and some who are
just downright inappropriate in their ability to meet targets. The Green Party fails to see
how the Vanguard Military School - style press -ups and military training punishment
model is going to create the best modern learning environment. That is not the
pedagogy of collaborative learning tha t we all believe in; it is the pedagogy of
authoritarian control.
It was very interesting when a professor from the University of Oregon talked in this
Parliament not long ago about how the authoritarian model, which appears to work in
Asia to create great Programme for International Student Assessment standards but does
not lead to innovative thinking, is welcomed by Western societies that do not know how
to manage kids without an authoritarian model. He said our biggest challenge was
creativity. In fact,  the Chinese Government and the Singaporeans, for example, are
recognising that it is not working, and that paths that test standardised teaching and
national standards for those countries are not creating innovative learners who can then
lead a modern world.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Again, not true.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: So it was really interesting to hear him speak. The
Minister says it is not true, but he was a fantastically creative person who has been
employed by the Chinese Government for that very reason—for that very reason.
The Green Party is very keen to work for solutions for genuine initiatives to become
part of quality public education in Aotearoa that is culturally appropriate and
innovative. That can happen, but we do not need to privatise. We do not need for -profit,
State-funded, unaccountable schools to do that.
Much of this bill is detail—and stuff that I would like to read in more detail —around
international students, private training associations, and te acher registration. Much of it
may well be useful. We often find that these omnibus bills combine things that are good
with things are that are actually abhorrent and then put us in a difficult position because
we cannot support them. We will be looking fo r the greater good in the bill if it is there,
but the overall approach towards the tertiary governance issues and towards the
education council is very disturbing. We find it difficult when our in -boxes are now
being flooded by people who are very concern ed about this bill and do not believe there
are enough good things in it to justify it.
It is difficult to imagine how less democracy and less teacher involvement in their
own professional body will result in better decision -making. Steven Joyce talks abo ut,
for example, cutting students out being a choice—people can choose to cut students out.
What he is failing to acknowledge is that democracy needs to be encouraged, supported,
and acknowledged in law so people recognise the importance of those diverse v oices
rather the myth of efficiency. [Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to
interrupt the member. I have been contemplating for some time. There is a longstanding
convention in the House —it goes back to the time of Sir Basil Arthur in 1984 —
Speaker’s ruling 63/1. When members are in close proximity to each other and there are
constant interjections going on, it actually has an effec t on the microphones, so I just
ask the member the Hon Hekia Parata to please desist.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: An education amendment bill is an opportunity to
strengthen democracy in education, and, unfortunately, this bill fails to do that.
16696 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is an enormous pleasure to take a brief call on
this bill. The Education Amendment Bill (No 2) is another strand in this Government’s
cable of initiatives to lift New Zeal anders’ educational achievement. I personally have
benefited hugely from our country’s education system. I went to Westown School in
New Plymouth. I went to that paragon of virtue—

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: Bastion of virtue.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: —of a secondary school, New Plymouth Boys’ High School.
The Hon Maryan Street went to the sister school across the river, New Plymouth Girls’
High School. I then went to Otago University, and the highest compliment I can pay to
Cambridge University, where I did my medical degree, was that it was as good as Otago
University but in a different way. Why do I mention Otago University? It was there that
I met a young man whose musical virtuosity left me absolutely in awe. I am talking
about Tim Haz ledine, who was a young economics student. Tim went on to become a
professor of economics, in fact, a member of the Auckland University council, and a
little bit of a comic, I have to say. It was something he had not displayed as a student.
He showed no sign of comic prowess. He was a brilliant musician and is still a brilliant
musician. But the reason I think he has perhaps indulged in stand -up comedy is that he
referred to Steven Joyce as an “old-fashioned socialist central planner at heart”. I do not
know what the Opposition feels about that, but I have a hard job equating the Steven
Joyce that I know with that sobriquet.
Why do I mention Tim? I mention Tim because I have a huge amount of respect for
him. He is an economist, and yet he finds the prospect  of slightly reducing the number
of people in a governance entity —to whit, the new university councils —and having
people on there with proven governance experience outrageous and remarkable. He says
there is no need for it —there is absolutely no need for i t. He does not give a skerrick of
evidence as to why there is no need for it. So what evidence can we find to suggest that
there may be need for it? Well, it does not come much simpler than looking at a past
experience where this happened, in 2009 when the  policies came in and were instituted
in 2010 by the Tertiary Education Commission in the Institutes of Technology and
Polytechnics—the ITPs. What happened when the Government introduced a policy like
this? We had the opportunity to hear from no less a per son than Tim Fowler, the chief
executive of the Tertiary Education Commission, who looked at what happened. What
Mr Fowler told us was that with the reduction in numbers of the councils of the ITPs
and with a requirement for skilled governance ability, in fact, the performance of these
organisations improved.
Are we surprised? We are not surprised. That was the commission’s impression and
its summary after a number of visits to them. So what did it do? It went back twice since
2010 and it is going to do so  again to evaluate the effectiveness and impact of the
changes. It has not just looked at the performance and found it to be much improved,
but it has also interviewed the new chairs, the chief executives, and the chief financial
officers of these organisa tions. The feedback from those individuals, who are actually
on the bodies, has been uniformly favourable. So there is evidence, hard evidence, that
this model works.
Before I close, I will just address a few points that have been raised. As the Minister
for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment himself said, this is about making
council membership requirements more flexible by removing specific representative
requirements. What can be bad about more freedom to make, involve, and create the
make-up of your local council in your university? I cannot see a problem with that. That
was one of the concerns raised by the Opposition. I could go on for ages, but time is
pressing. I look forward to further debate on this bill in future.
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16697

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. I would like to
acknowledge Dr Cam Calder, who is the chair of the Education and Science Committee.
He is a lovely man, and he is going to have a hell of a time on that commit tee, around
the Education Amendment Bill (No 2). I want to acknowledge Dr Calder now, because I
want to make sure he understands that although I appreciate his collegial manner on the
select committee it will not last with this bill.
I would like to start at the beginning. Let us just note bullet point No. 2 in the general
policy statement, which says: “to create a regulatory framework that promotes
accountability and high standards within the education sector;”. The National
Government just cannot seem to  help itself. Either that, or it just does not realise how
insulting that truly is to hard -working professionals inside education in this country.
Statements like that suggest to the public that there currently is not any accountability or
that the profess ion does not already have high standards, otherwise the bill would not
say to create them. Any Minister with actual knowledge of this sector would have
known that that statement is demonstrably false and would not have allowed the staff to
use that language.
It is farcical to suggest later in this bill that one of the purposes of creating the new
Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand is to raise the status of the teaching
profession. It is farcical because it is this Government that has done more damag e to the
status of the teaching profession than any other single incident or entity since it began
using attacks on this profession for political purposes in 2008. This Government makes
these sorts of derogatory statements inside legislation, which places them on the
permanent historical record of this House, and then it has the audacity to try to kiss up
to teachers by launching a website where people write on it about their personal
favourite teacher.
The Government has announced a top -down bribe of $359  million, in an attempt to
get teachers to forget the number of times the Government has kicked them in the guts
over the close to 6 years that we have had this National Government. The Government
appears to hope that teachers will be so busy trying to fig ure out their payslips from
Novopay that they will not notice that legislation like this will remove their
representation on a body that they will be paying for. According to Treasury papers,
they will be paying more for the privilege of having this Govern ment take away their
ability to elect their representatives.
If this bill is not about raising the status of the sector, then what is the purpose of
these changes? The Minister of Education has been very helpful in her publicly
recorded statements. This i s unusual, but she has. Ms Parata uses dog whistle politics
when she makes statements such as: “There will be less chance of dodgy teachers
resurfacing at other schools under this legislation.” What absolute rubbish. The Minister
knows that one of the wors t convicted sex offenders was found to have completely
bypassed the teacher registration process, so nothing inside this bill will stop that from
happening again.
The Minister seeks to remove the basic rights of teachers around being innocent until
proven guilty, through clauses in this legislation. Teachers are humans too. They
deserve the right to be able to have complaints against them heard away from the public,
until it is shown that that complaint has a basis in truth. Teachers will be pursued, under
this legislation, and the Minister is using that to try to create turmoil and a voting base
for the National Party, just as it did when it scaremongered in 2008 and just as it did
when it scaremongered in 2011. The Minister knows that it is more likely th at
improvements to the front end of teacher training, through the screening of potential
teacher trainee candidates and the continual screening of candidates, around a holistic
16698 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
matrix, would have more effect, as opposed to the current “bums on seats”
mismanagement of teacher supply in practice under this Government.
The Minister knows that her Government has left a gap that one could drive a truck
through. It specifically puts our children at risk in recent charter school amendments to
this same bill that allow anyone with a Ministry of Justice check into those charter
school classrooms. The fact that the Ministry of Justice checks cover only New Zealand
convictions, and not those from overseas, has been ignored by this Minister and by this
Government. The fact that should any incident arise in a charter school around any of
these individuals, where there is no central record to track them from one charter school
to another, puts our children at risk. But the Minister does not want the New Zealand
public to focus on that.
This Government prefers to have another go at the professional body that actually
takes the educating of our young people seriously. If I have a criticism of members of
the teaching profession in New Zealand, it is that they are too reasona ble. They try too
hard to accommodate the many choices that this Government says it wants for our
children. If there is a criticism I have of them, it is that they are so invested in the
children of this country that they put themselves so far second and t hey have allowed
this Government to ride roughshod over them.
But they do stand up, so why do the Minister and the Government pursue this
legislation? It is about the fact that the teaching profession is still fighting back.
Teachers still stand up, no ma tter how battered and bruised they are, and they fight for
their students to be judged as a whole person, on holistic criteria, as opposed to the
narrow robotic view the National Party would like. The National Party believes only in
winners and losers. Tha t is its reality. Given a chance, we believe, this Government
would bring back the “scale to fail” of the 1970s. We believe that this Government
would have primary school children held back, year upon year, if they did not meet the
national standards.
We have seen no money being put into the front end of the spend, to support students
who have been clearly identified, which is what the purpose of national standards was
supposed to be when it was sold to this country in 2008. Not a single cent of the close to
$40 million spent to date on national standards has touched a child at the front end and
given more resources with regard to our dyslexic children, our dyspraxic children, and
our children who need any other support —not a single cent. If this is not abo ut
protecting our children, and it is not about lifting the status of the profession, what is it
actually about? Again, Minister Parata has articulated this —mistakenly perhaps, but
none the less she has put it into the public domain. This is about control.  This is about
removing any elected official from the body of the profession and giving the Minister
total control of all appointments. The Minister has quite clearly told the educational
representation bodies that her ultimate goal is that this new counci l will be the only
body that she or any future Minister of Education will have to consult when they start
the next tranche of privatisation and performance pay amendments to our education
system.
But Minister Parata is not the only member of this Governme nt who is hell -bent on
removing democracy and the need to consult from the education sector, so let us move
on to the amendments in the bill under Mr Steven Joyce’s area. We have seen that it is
about removing what this Government finds most annoying. It i s about the requirement
to consult, and removing it. We have seen time and time again from this Government —
and it is an arrogance that is inherent in the National Party —a disdain to enter into
constructive dialogue. This is why this party actually finds it  most difficult to get its
head around MMP. MMP is actually about entering into constructive dialogue and this
party finds it very difficult to do so.
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16699
Well, we all know that it is much easier for people to just do as they are told. We
know that. But that is called a dictatorship, and history has shown us time and time
again that the people will stand a dictatorship for only so long before they will demand
to have their views and their voice heard, and we hope that the New Zealand public will
demand that th eir voice be heard later this year. Mr Joyce is basically saying that we
should trust him with his ministerial appointments, and I am sure my Opposition
colleagues will address this further as they go on.
I want to have a look today, in the last few minut es, at the performance of this
particular Minister. Informatio n provided to us about the make -up of the current
ministerial appointments to councils show that he cannot be trusted to actually provide
the diversity that is required to keep these councils re presentative. At the moment only
16 percent of his appointments are women, only one Māori, and no Pasifika. Two -thirds
of his appointments have been chief executive officers, company directors, or
accountants; a further 20 percent are commercial lawyers; a nd only four come from
some other professional background. And this is despite 90 percent of graduates
actually heading into professions and vocations other than those.
The bill is a mishmash and we will stop it.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on the first
reading of the Education Amendment Bill (No 2). I intend to take only a brief call
because I look forward to the opportunity of receiving submissions from the parties who
are interested.
This bill certainly fits in with the Better Public Services targets that this Government
has set out. It proposes to establish a new professional body for the education
profession. It also intends to support the tertiary education instit utions with a better
governance structure. It will also codify a better pastoral care model for international
education. And it will also reinforce the New Zealand Qualifications Authority side of
appraising the delivery of quality assurance of tertiary in stitutions. So I look forward to
receiving those submissions.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Will it make a difference? Will it matter?

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: I would also say, just as a point of conclusion, that what we are
hearing from the other side t otally ignores the underperformance of a lot of our
institutions in the way that they have delivered outcomes and qualifications to our
students. When we reflect on the way that the taxpayer dollar is spent, we should be
very, very careful that we deliver quality for that taxpayer dollar. I have great pleasure
in supporting this bill.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: You have to hand it to this
Government for its consistency. There are a couple of areas  of consistency that I am
going to talk about today. This is a Government that when it does not like what people
who are elected to a body are doing, simply does away with voting. It has literally taken
away votes where I come from in Christchurch —we no longer have an elected regional
council. But in education this Government has really taken the knife to the notion of
representation. We have seen it with charter schools, which are not going to have
elected boards of trustees, taking away the rights of comm unities to have a say in how
these schools are run. We have seen this with the closures and mergers, and the creation
of super-schools in Christchurch. Bigger schools mean less community governance and
less community representation within our election system.
Moving right along, this Government is now taking the knife even further into the
notion of representation in our education system in the tertiary sector. We are seeing it
in the Teachers Council and we are seeing it in our university councils. When t his
Government does not like something that it is being told, it simply gets rid of the elected
members. It just does not like it. It just simply appoints some of its friends. It puts into
16700 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
positions some of its friends who will roll and do exactly what the y want. We look at
Environment Canterbury and water irrigation —put in commissioners who will agree
with that. You want things to happen; you appoint your mates who will not put up one
murmur of discontent about what is going to happen. This is a Government  that has
given up on the notion that we elect people through democratic means and that this is an
effective way of having governance. This is a Government that has given up on the idea
of any type of civic governance, it seems, in education and simply wan ts to rule through
corporate models.
Well, newsflash—it is not a company. These are universities, these are our schools,
and corporate governance is not necessarily the best model.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: But Government is business, Megan.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: “But Government is business.” my colleague tells me. Well,
that is the way it is being treated by this Government.
Let us go through some of that changes that are going to be made. I did say I was
going to talk about consistency in two areas from this Government. I just want to go
through its capacity to botch - up everything in education. I will take just 1 year—1 year
out of the 5 long years, nearly 6 long years, it has been in Government —and have a
look at the number of botch -ups. Let us pick a year, any year —2012 will do. In May
2012 larger class sizes were announced. In June this was reversed. The Minister of
Education had got it wrong. In August the Minister’s top adviser quits. In September the
Canterbury school closures are an nounced. In October it seems her cousin is behind the
charter schools. In November there was the Novopay debacle. In December the
Christchurch teachers decide to go on strike. In December Lesley Longstone resigns.
This is a Government with the capacity to turn absolutely everything it touches in
education to absolute custard.
We have that again with this omnibus bill, the Education Amendment Bill (No 2),
which we have been presented with. This is a bill that came to the House on Monday.
We are debating it now, on Thursday. It covers off very large areas of disparate bits of
our education system. What is it that the Government is trying to hide? What is it that
the Government is trying to do? What we have is a very consistent theme. They may be
disparate par ts of our education system, but we have a very consistent theme of an
arrogant and out of touch Government that is interested only in appointing its mates to
key positions.
Let us have a look at the Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand and what
these changes will do. Well, this is a Government that does not believe that the council
should be representative of the sector. What we believe in and what we stand for on this
side of the House is a democratically elected educational council. Hekia Parata has  been
heavy-handed in all the decisions she has made, and this is another one. I want a
Government member to take more than a 1 -minute call on this bill and tell us why it is
that teachers should not and do not need to be on this council. Why is it that we  do not
need to have teachers on it?
Moving right through to the tertiary sector, Steven Joyce is hiding in Hekia Parata’s
bill. It must be that he senses a botch -up and knows that one more against Hekia
Parata’s name is not going to make a blind bit of d ifference. So let us have a look.
Steven Joyce tells us it is OK because universities can still choose to have students and
staff on their governing bodies. Well, that is not good enough, Mr Joyce. What we say
is there needs to be legislative protections s o that the governing bodies of our
universities will ensure that the people who work in universities and teach in them, the
colleagues of the collegial body that makes up a university, have a voice and a say in
how a university is run. We also say there ne eds to be legislative protection for people
who attend those colleges, who are taught by those colleagues in these collegial
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16701
environments, to have a say in how universities are run. We have had no justification
for why we are going to change an age-old tradition of how a university is run.
If you go back to the very reason that democratic councils and bodies were
established in universities, you go back to the beginning of the 19 th century, when they
were put in place to ensure that we entrenched Enlighten ment thinking and teaching
within our universities and that we did not hark back to religious tuition within our
universities. The only way this could be protected was by having the people with a real
stake in it have a say in the running of those universi ties. We have had absolutely no
justification. We have the regulatory impact statement on this aspect of the bill, which
really cannot give the Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment any
arguments that he needs to argue for it.
My colleagu e Grant Robertson has been looking through the size of some of the
governing bodies of universities throughout the world. The Minister is telling us we
need to make this massive reduction down to 8 to 12 people on our governing bodies so
that we can have better universities, we can be better at innovating, and we can be better
academics. Well, go tell that to Stanford University, with 38 members on its governing
body. Go tell that to Harvard, with 32. Go tell that to Oxford University, with 30. Go
tell that  to Cambridge University, which has 16 places reserved for academic staff
members on its governing body. It has a further three places reserved for students
because it makes that university a better place. Then we have the Massachusetts
Institute of Technology with its 76. Well, that university is pretty shoddy at innovation
and commercialisation, is it not? We must need to change it.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Hopeless!

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is a hopeless university —need to change tha t! The
Minister will not even talk about the report that he received in 2012 from the Ministry
of Education. What was the Minister told in this report that he received in 2012? Well,
it was noted that, internationally, even those bodies that were taking a skills-based
approach maintained stakeholder representation in their governance —that even if you
do want to go to a smaller model, you do not have to do away with staff representation
and you do not have to do away with student representation.
But this Minister has made a decision. This Minister knows that it is the staff who are
not putting up with the way in which he sees education as a cost to be cut, and that the
staff on those councils are not happy with the money that he is taking away from those
institutions and the fact that he sees success in tertiary education as dampening down
the demand for tertiary education. He certainly does not want students sitting on those
governing bodies because, heck, some of those students might be people who have had
their access to allowances and loans cut. This is a Minister who is taking the knife to
tertiary education, and he does not want to have critics. He does not want universities to
carry out their very function as the critics and conscience of society.
This is a Government that is continuing its grand tradition now of taking away
democratic rights when it does not like what someone is saying. All New Zealanders
should be very worried because this is something we are seeing right throughout our
country in var ious places. Elected staff members and students should have a say.
Teachers should have a say. Education is too important to leave to Steven Joyce and
Hekia Parata.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): Well, it is interesting; you have to be
very careful with the facts coming from the other side. One of my colleagues was
pointing out, I think, that five of the las t six graphics the Labour Party has put up on its
Twitter feed and Facebook have been wrong. You know, details have to be right and
precise. Let us talk about a quick example —a quick example to give context. I was at a
school recently, talking to a teacher . She came up to me and said: “Simon, I vote
16702 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 13 Mar 2014
Labour. I’m a union person. I always vote Labour. I can’t bring myself to vote for
National in education.” But she said: “You know what? Actually, National is doing the
right thing in education. The $350 million  - plus you are putting in to support teachers
and the other elements you’re putting in to support young people are incredibly
important.” That was from a person who is an avowed voter for the left. She knew that
this Government is doing the right thing.
The Education Amendment Bill (No 2), looking at the Education Council of
Aotearoa New Zealand, is doing the right thing. It is doing the right thing. [Interruption]
Here we go. Members on the other side are saying we are making it up again —a lack of

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I want to make  a few points.
First of all, I will respond to the member Simon O’Connor, who just sat down. I actually
agree that some of the changes that National is making are useful. I think the $359
million is a step in the right direction, but one has got to remembe r that it is well under
1 percent of the salary budget. It is minuscule and actually will not make the changes
that National wants.
We in the Labour Party will vote against this bill, the Education Amendment Bill
(No 2). The main reason that I am voting a gainst this bill is as a result of the changes
that were made around tertiary education governance. I think that if there had been two
bills and this bill addressed only the question of the Education Council of Aotearoa
New Zealand, then it could well be amendable and supportable.
I think it is fair to say, as a former Minister of Education, that probably my biggest
area of policy failure was the setting up in the initial stages of the New Zealand
Teachers Council. It was something where the initial appoin tment was wrong. Kathie
Irwin was not a suitable person to appoint to chair that organisation. I took advice on the
matter, and I had doubts. The advice came from Liz Gordon, and I regret that I took her
advice as to Kathie’s suitability, because my view w as that the Teachers Council
probably suffered for a period of about 5 years as a result of the poor governance at the
beginning of the process and the poor setting up then.
I do want to acknowledge the recent work that Stan Rodger did in tidying up some of
it, and, more recently, Kathy Smith and Alison McAlpine. As chairs of the organisation
they have done a very good job. I also want to acknowledge the current chief executive,
who I think has done an excellent job and has almost certainly been the best. Having
criticised Kathie Irwin, I have to say that my old mate Harvey McQueen did not have
the ability to do the necessary detailed work and to set the necessary systems up. Even
his recollections of the time of the Lange Government were a relatively poor history.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: He was a poet , and he had imagination. He had
imagination in his writings, and I think it is fair to say that he did not have the necessary
focus to be the c hief executive of an organisation like the Teachers Council, and that is
sad. I think that as a result of that it did suffer and the vision that I had for it —which
was that it would, in fact, be the organisation that was the main deliverer of professional
learning for teachers in New Zealand; that it would contract with the Ministry of
Education; and that it would be the organisation that would be of teachers, by teachers,
for teachers, and for developing the profession —is something that we have lost by a
period of, probably, about 15 years. That is something that I very much regret. My
13 Mar 2014 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 16703
colleagues will tell other members of the House that it is not that often you get a mea
culpa from me, but in this particular area I think we did lose something.
My view is also that if we had managed to make the transfer of the funding of
professional learning to the Teachers Council, it would not have been as easy for Anne
Tolley to take that $100 million out in the way that she did on an annual basis in the
first of those budgets. My view is that that sort of cut —if it was to an organisation that
was owned by teachers and contracted to teachers—would have resulted in much louder
screams than actually occurred. The screams in 2009 were mainly political. They were
not extensive screams.
My view is that most parents did not realise that the National Government was
cutting the future quality of the education of young people in New Zealand by taking
out the funding for the most important thing. The quality of learning in a class room is
very much based on the quality of teaching, and the quality of teaching depends on the
professional development and the professional support of those teachers. The National
Government cut that to ribbons in its first term. I think our kids will suf fer for decades
